title: Development money handed to private equity and for-profit hospitals
conviction: The collapse of Abraaj, backed by the Gates Foundation and development banks, led to US fraud charges and guilty pleas; Oxfam documented hospitals funded by development banks detaining patients who could not pay. That development lenders' turn to private equity routinely lets money meant for the poor be skimmed or spent on care the poor cannot reach is the suspicion.
story: In early 2018 four investors in a $1 billion health fund, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the World Bank's private-sector arm the International Finance Corporation, Britain's CDC Group and France's Proparco, hired forensic accountants to find out what had happened to about $200 million they had put in to build hospitals and clinics in poor countries such as Pakistan, India and Nigeria. The fund was run by the Abraaj Group, a Dubai private equity firm that managed almost $14 billion and whose founder, Arif Naqvi, had sat on a Davos panel with Bill Gates. Within months Abraaj collapsed in what Bloomberg called the world's biggest private-equity insolvency. In 2019 US prosecutors charged Naqvi and other executives with defrauding investors, and two former partners pleaded guilty. A British judge approved Naqvi's extradition in 2021, and in March 2023 the High Court refused his last challenge; he denies the charges. The suspicion is that, as aid agencies and development banks hand more of their money to private equity funds and for-profit companies, money meant for the poor is skimmed off in fees and fraud or spent on services the poor cannot afford, with little oversight.

Oxfam looked at where the money reached hospitals. In 2023 Oxfam traced more than 350 health investments made by the development finance arms of Britain, France, Germany, the European Union and the World Bank. It found that the Nairobi Women's Hospital in Kenya, funded by several of them, had held patients, including a newborn baby and a schoolboy, for months until their bills were paid, and had kept the body of one woman's mother for two years. In Lagos, the most basic maternity package at the funded Lagoon Hospitals cost more than nine years' income for the poorest tenth of Nigerians. Oxfam could not find a single disclosed evaluation that credibly measured what these investments did for low-income patients.

The investments often pass through layers of funds, and Oxfam reported that the development banks invest in the same health companies through the same intermediaries, many in tax havens, as this map's entry on development money flowing through tax havens describes. At an Indian chain backed by three of the lenders, CARE Hospitals, a family told Oxfam their injured child was refused treatment unless they paid $1,200; TPG, a shareholder in the chain, told Oxfam that patients are always treated in an emergency whatever their finances. The IFC told the Guardian that private providers can add to health systems' capacity.

What would settle it is disclosure, fund by fund, of how much development money went into private equity and for-profit health companies, what fees the fund managers took, and who the patients turned out to be, with independent audits of the funds' accounts. Abraaj's books were checked only after investors noticed money sitting unspent.
missing: No fund-by-fund disclosure of development money in private equity, the fees taken, or who was served.
would_settle: Fund-level disclosure of development-bank money placed with private equity and for-profit health firms, management fees, independent audits and patient income data.

title: Credit ratings that punish poor countries for seeking debt relief
conviction: Rating agencies downgraded Ethiopia for applying to the G20's debt relief scheme; a UNDP study puts the cost of subjective ratings to 19 African countries at $74.5 billion; S&P and Moody's paid over $2 billion over inflated ratings for paying clients. That the agencies systematically protect private creditors at poor countries' expense is the suspicion.
story: On 29 January 2021 Ethiopia announced that it would ask for debt relief under the G20's new Common Framework, the scheme rich governments had set up so the poorest countries could restructure what they owed. On 9 February Fitch cut Ethiopia's rating from B to CCC, saying the request explicitly raised the risk of default. In March Moody's put Ethiopia on review for a downgrade, because the framework would require it to seek similar relief from private lenders, and in May it cut Ethiopia to Caa1. S&P also downgraded. Ethiopia's bonds fell, making any future borrowing dearer. The economist Jayati Ghosh wrote that governments would now fear entering talks with private creditors even within programmes designed to help them. Three firms, S&P, Moody's and Fitch, issue more than 90 per cent of outstanding credit ratings. The suspicion is that these agencies judge poor countries, and African ones above all, more harshly than the facts justify, and punish governments that try to cut their debts, in ways that protect the private investors who are their main audience while raising the cost of borrowing for the countries.

In 2023 the UN Development Programme studied the ratings of African countries. It estimated that if ratings were based on less subjective judgements, 19 African countries could save up to $74.5 billion in excess interest and lost lending, more than the continent receives in aid each year. Hippolyte Fofack, chief economist of the African Export-Import Bank, wrote in 2021 that more than half of rated African countries were downgraded in 2020, against a global average of 31.8 per cent. UNDP said the costs could arise from thin data and subjective methods rather than conscious bias, and its study found the agencies use similar methods worldwide.

The two largest agencies have paid to settle claims over inflated ratings. In 2015 S&P paid $1.375 billion and in 2017 Moody's paid about $864 million to settle US federal and state claims over their ratings of mortgage securities before the 2008 crash. Connecticut's attorney general said the states had alleged that Moody's ratings were influenced by the demands of the banks that issued the securities and paid for the ratings. Both firms accepted statements of facts and neither admitted breaking the law. The African Development Bank's president has called for Africa to have its own credit rating agency.

What would settle it is a full comparison of how the agencies rate African and other poor countries against richer countries with the same debt, growth and repayment record, and of every downgrade that followed a request for debt relief, with the agencies' internal committee notes. Those notes are not published.
missing: No published comparison of ratings for poor and rich countries with matching fundamentals; rating committee notes are private.
would_settle: Rating committee records and a matched comparison of ratings for poor versus richer countries with similar fundamentals, including all downgrades following debt-relief requests.

conviction: Ecuador's and Belize's swaps were funded by bonds Credit Suisse arranged, with binding conservation terms, and private members hold six of eleven seats on Ecuador's Galápagos fund; Galápagos groups complained to the IDB over lack of information. That these deals serve bankers and foreign conservation groups more than the countries is the suspicion.
story: In May 2023 Ecuador announced what was called the largest debt-for-nature swap in history. Credit Suisse, the Swiss bank, bought back $1.63 billion of Ecuador's bonds from investors at between 35.5 and 53.25 cents on the dollar, after a political crisis had driven their price down. To pay for it, a company set up in Ireland, GPS Blue Financing, sold $656 million of new 'Galápagos marine bonds' to investors and lent the money to Ecuador. Because the US government's development bank insured the deal and the Inter-American Development Bank guaranteed part of it, Moody's rated the new bonds Aa2, among its highest grades, while Ecuador's own bonds were rated junk. In return Ecuador committed to spend about $12 million a year on marine conservation in the Galápagos for almost two decades, through a new fund, the Galápagos Life Fund, on whose 11-member board, according to the Latin American network Latindadd, six seats went to private and non-government members. In 2024 Galápagos community groups complained to the Inter-American Development Bank's watchdog that they had been given too little information and no say; the finance ministry did not provide all the financial documents a local rights group requested. The suspicion is that these swaps, sold as debt relief for nature, are designed around the fees and safe returns of bankers and the control of foreign conservation groups, with small savings for the country and decisions over its own waters and forests moved outside its government.

Belize's deal in 2021 set the model. A subsidiary of the US charity The Nature Conservancy lent Belize the money to buy back its $553 million 'superbond' at 55 cents on the dollar, funded by bonds Credit Suisse arranged and insured by the US development bank. In return Belize legally committed to protect 30 per cent of its ocean by 2026, up from 15.9 per cent, and to spend about $4 million a year on marine conservation until 2041, with higher payments if it misses the targets. Belize's debt fell by about a tenth of its national income.

Similar deals followed in Barbados, Gabon, the Bahamas and, in 2024, Ecuador's Amazon. In January 2023 Barclays questioned in a note to investors whether such swaps deserve their green label, since only a small part of the money raised reaches conservation; other critics point to the arrangers' fees and the cost of the insurance, neither fully published. Credit Suisse, which arranged the largest, collapsed and was taken over by UBS in 2023.

What would settle it is publication of the full terms of each swap: fees and insurance premiums, what the country saved after all costs, who sits on each conservation fund and what they can decide, and what local communities were told before signing. Ecuador's Galápagos papers were requested under freedom-of-information law and not all were released.
missing: Full fees, insurance costs and net savings of each swap are not published.
would_settle: Published fees, insurance premiums, net fiscal savings and governance rules for each debt-for-nature swap, with records of local consultation.

title: Foreign companies that pay soldiers and militias to protect their profits
conviction: Chiquita and Lafarge pleaded guilty in US courts to paying groups designated as terrorists; company records showed Freeport paying Indonesian officers; Amnesty documented Shell's payments to Nigeria's security forces. That foreign companies routinely pay armed men who then kill local people is the suspicion.
story: In March 2007 Chiquita Brands, the American banana company, pleaded guilty in a US federal court to paying a Colombian paramilitary group, the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, known as the AUC. Through its Colombian subsidiary, Banadex, Chiquita had paid the AUC more than $1.7 million between 1997 and 2004 in the banana-growing regions of Urabá and Santa Marta, where the group was killing civilians, and the company kept paying more than $300,000 after the US Justice Department told it to stop. Chiquita paid a $25 million fine. Thousands of Colombians later sued over relatives killed by the group, and in June 2024 a federal jury in Florida found Chiquita liable for eight of those killings and ordered it to pay $38.3 million to their families. The suspicion is that foreign companies operating in poor and conflict-ridden countries routinely pay soldiers, police and militias to guard their mines, plantations and pipelines, knowing that the same men kill, beat and drive off the people who live nearby.

In December 2005 the New York Times reported, from company records, that the American mining company Freeport-McMoRan had given Indonesian military and police generals, colonels, majors, captains and units nearly $20 million between 1998 and 2004 around its Grasberg copper and gold mine in Papua, besides money for barracks and roads. Freeport said it had no alternative to relying on Indonesia's military and police, and that its payments were legal. In April 1995 the Australian Council for Overseas Aid had reported that at least 37 people, 22 of them civilians, were killed or disappeared around the mine in 1994 and early 1995, and that Freeport security staff joined the army in shootings, arrests and torture; Freeport and the Indonesian government denied the death figures.

In 2017 Amnesty International published a report drawing on thousands of pages of Shell's internal documents from Nigeria in the 1990s, when the Ogoni people were protesting against the company's oil pollution. Amnesty found that Shell had given the security forces logistical support and payments, which the head of Shell Nigeria from 1994 admitted was standard practice, and that it kept asking for military help after security forces had killed protesters and burned villages; Shell said it never colluded with the military or encouraged violence. In October 2022 the French cement company Lafarge pleaded guilty in the United States to paying the Islamic State and the al-Nusrah Front, through intermediaries, about $6 million in 2013 and 2014 to keep its $680 million plant in northern Syria running, and agreed to pay about $778 million. US officials said it was the first time a company had pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organisation.

These payments came out through prosecutions, a newspaper's access to company records and a human rights group's access to internal files. Companies are generally not required to publish what they pay to security forces abroad. What would settle how common this is would be mandatory, country-by-country disclosure of payments to soldiers, police and private armed groups by every company operating in conflict areas, matched against records of killings and evictions around their sites.
missing: No mandatory disclosure of company payments to security forces and armed groups abroad.
would_settle: Country-by-country disclosure of payments to soldiers, police and armed groups by companies in conflict areas, matched to records of killings and evictions near their sites.

title: Foreign companies behind the overthrow of governments
conviction: Declassified CIA histories confirm the 1953 Iran coup followed the nationalisation of a British oil company and the 1954 Guatemala coup followed land reform against United Fruit; a US Senate inquiry found ITT offered the CIA $1 million against Allende. That companies with large investments still help remove governments that threaten them is the suspicion.
story: In 1952 Guatemala's elected president, Jacobo Árbenz, passed a land reform, Decree 900, that took uncultivated land from large estates and gave it to landless farmers. The biggest landowner was the American United Fruit Company, which held a large share of the country's farmland and left most of it unplanted. The government took hundreds of thousands of acres of the company's idle land and offered compensation based on the value United Fruit itself had declared for tax. The company lobbied Washington and spread the claim that Árbenz was a communist. In June 1954 a small force led by Carlos Castillo Armas invaded from Honduras, organised and armed by the CIA in an operation it called PBSUCCESS, and Árbenz resigned; Castillo Armas cancelled the land reform and returned the land to United Fruit. The CIA's own history of the operation, written in the 1990s, was later declassified. Some historians say the US acted mainly out of fear of communism and that there is no proof United Fruit organised the coup. The suspicion is that large foreign companies have repeatedly helped bring down governments that threatened their investments, using their own governments' spy agencies to do it, and that this has not stopped.

Iran's coup had come a year earlier. In May 1951 Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh nationalised the British-owned Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, the forerunner of BP. In August 1953 he was overthrown. In 2013 the CIA released an internal history stating that the coup was carried out under CIA direction as an act of US foreign policy, with British help; it also showed the CIA arranging $5 million for the new government within days. Britain has never officially acknowledged its part, and British officials in the 1970s tried to stop the US releasing documents that would embarrass the UK.

In Chile, a 1973 US Senate subcommittee on multinational corporations found that the American telephone company ITT, which feared that Salvador Allende would nationalise its Chilean company, had offered the CIA $1 million in 1970 to help stop him becoming president. The offer was turned down, while the CIA ran its own operations against Allende. In 1978 two ITT officials were charged with lying to the Senate about the company's actions in Chile; in 1979 the government dropped the case against one of them, Robert Berrellez, saying a trial would expose national security information. This map's entry on loans cut off to bring down governments tells what the US government did to Chile's lending at the same time.

These cases came out decades later, through congressional inquiries and declassified files. What would settle whether companies still play this part are the intelligence and foreign-ministry records of more recent coups and attempted coups in countries with large foreign investments, and the lobbying records of the companies involved, many of which remain classified or private.
missing: Few declassified records on company involvement in coups after the 1970s.
would_settle: Declassified intelligence and foreign-ministry records, plus company lobbying records, for recent coups and attempts in countries with large foreign investments.

title: Private tribunals that can order countries to pay companies billions
conviction: Investor-state tribunals have ordered Pakistan to pay $5.9 billion and Ecuador $1.77 billion; a study found 15 arbitrators decided 55% of known cases. That the system is run by a small club of lawyers that favours investors and deters governments from regulating is the suspicion.
story: On 12 July 2019 a tribunal at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, part of the World Bank Group, ordered Pakistan to pay $5.976 billion to Tethyan Copper, a company owned by the Canadian miner Barrick Gold and Chile's Antofagasta. Pakistan's province of Balochistan refused Tethyan a lease in November 2011 to mine Reko Diq, one of the world's largest untouched copper and gold deposits, and in 2013 Pakistan's Supreme Court declared the original deal void. The tribunal held that Pakistan had treated the company unfairly and awarded $4.087 billion for the mine's value plus interest and costs, a sum equal to about 2 per cent of Pakistan's national income and almost the size of the $6 billion loan the IMF had just agreed to lend Pakistan. Reuters reported that the company had invested more than $220 million in the project; its owners have put their spending at more than $500 million. In 2022 Pakistan settled: the award was dropped, Barrick took 50 per cent of a revived mine, and Pakistani state companies paid Antofagasta $900 million to leave. The suspicion is that the system of investor-state tribunals, written into thousands of investment treaties, lets foreign companies override national courts and laws in private hearings, run by a small group of lawyers who profit from the cases, so that poor countries pay billions or give in rather than regulate.

Ecuador was ordered in October 2012 to pay the American oil company Occidental $1.77 billion, $2.3 billion with interest, then the largest award in the centre's history, after Ecuador ended Occidental's contract for an Amazon oil block in 2006 because the company had transferred part of its stake to another firm without government approval, as the contract required. One of the three arbitrators dissented. In 2015 a review committee cut the award to about $1 billion, which Ecuador paid.

A 2012 study by Corporate Europe Observatory and the Transnational Institute, Profiting from Injustice, found that 15 arbitrators, nearly all from Europe, the United States or Canada, had decided 55 per cent of all known investment-treaty disputes, and that several prominent arbitrators had sat on the boards of multinational companies, including some that had sued developing countries. Arbitrators at the centre are paid by the hour, and the same lawyers often act as arbitrator in one case and as counsel in another. Defenders of the system point out that, by UNCTAD's count, states win more concluded cases than investors, about 38 per cent against 29 per cent, and that each side chooses one of the three arbitrators. This map's documented pattern on companies suing states counts the claims.

The awards are published only in some cases, and the cost to governments of laws never passed for fear of being sued cannot be seen at all. What would settle the question is full publication of every case, the arbitrators' financial ties to the companies and law firms involved, and a record of regulations that governments withdrew or weakened after a company threatened a claim.
missing: Not all awards are published; arbitrators' ties are not publicly disclosed; laws withdrawn under threat of claims are unrecorded.
would_settle: Full publication of all investor-state cases, arbitrators' financial ties, and a record of regulations withdrawn after threatened claims.

title: Cities' water handed to foreign companies on the lenders' advice
conviction: World Bank lending and advice preceded water privatisations in Cochabamba, Jakarta and Manila, followed by sharp price rises, a fatal protest, and court and arbitration fights. That lenders pushed water privatisation for the benefit of a few multinationals is the suspicion.
story: In September 1999 the Bolivian government, in a process with a single bidder, gave the water system of Cochabamba, the country's third city, to Aguas del Tunari, a company controlled through offshore holdings by the American engineering company Bechtel, on a 40-year contract. According to the Democracy Center, a $14 million World Bank water loan had been conditioned on the city privatising its water. Within weeks bills rose by more than half on average, and in some homes by up to 200 per cent, in a country where the minimum wage was about $60 a month. Protests spread across the city, and in April 2000 the government declared a state of siege, soldiers shot dead a 17-year-old, Víctor Hugo Daza, and more than a hundred people were wounded, and the company left. Its owners moved its registration to the Netherlands to use a Dutch investment treaty and claimed at least $50 million from Bolivia at the World Bank's arbitration centre, having invested, by one estimate, less than $1 million; after an international campaign Bechtel and its Spanish partner Abengoa dropped the claim in January 2006 for a token two bolivianos, about 30 cents. The suspicion is that the World Bank and other lenders pushed poor countries to hand their cities' water to a handful of foreign companies, through loan conditions and advice, and that the companies profited while poor households paid more for water that did not improve.

Jakarta's water went the same way earlier. The World Bank lent Jakarta's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation; a 1998 Bank report said the loan had facilitated it. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and France's Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity and ordered it ended.

In Manila, the World Bank's private-sector arm, the International Finance Corporation, drafted the 1997 concession agreement under a contract that paid it at least $1 million if the bidding succeeded, and later bought into one of the winning companies. Basic rates in the east zone rose 496 per cent between 1997 and 2003, and from late October 2003, 672 people in the poor Tondo district fell ill with gastroenteritis after the west zone operator, part-owned by Suez, allegedly lowered water pressure. Coverage did rise, from about 60 to over 80 per cent of people by 2002.

The published record shows lending, advice and, in Cochabamba, a reported loan condition, but not who drafted the advice or which companies were consulted beforehand. What would settle the question is the internal correspondence of the lenders on water privatisations in the 1990s and 2000s, set beside the list of companies that won the contracts and the advisory fees the lenders' own arms earned.
missing: Internal lender correspondence on water privatisations and the companies consulted is unpublished.
would_settle: Lender correspondence on 1990s-2000s water privatisations, set against the companies that won and the advisory fees earned by the lenders' own arms.
